## How problems are packaged

Every finite MDP comes as a `DiscreteMDP` with five fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `T` | Transition array: `T[s, a, s′]` $= T(s' \mid s, a)$ |
| `R` | Reward array: `R[s, a]` $= R(s, a)$ |
| `gamma` (Python), `γ` (Julia) | Discount factor |
| `states` | A readable label for each state index, such as a tile's `(row, col)` |
| `actions` | A readable label for each action index, such as `"NE"` |

: Fields of a `DiscreteMDP`. The arrays use the same layout as [Chapter 7](../part2/ch07-exact-solution-methods.qmd). {#tbl-fields}

So any solver written for `(T, R, γ)` works on any problem. For example, here is Chapter 7's value iteration solving Hex World:

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
## Python

::: {#04c5a044 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from adm.mdp import greedy, value_iteration
from adm.problems.hex_world import hex_world

mdp = hex_world()
U, _ = value_iteration(mdp.T, mdp.R, mdp.gamma)
policy, _ = greedy(mdp.T, mdp.R, mdp.gamma, U)
```
:::


## Julia
```{.julia .snippet}
using ADM

mdp = hex_world()    # fields: T, R, γ, states, actions

# Value iteration (Ch 7): repeat Bellman backups until the values settle.
function solve(m; δ = 1e-6)
    U = zeros(length(m.states))
    while true
        Q = [m.R[s, a] + m.γ * sum(m.T[s, a, :] .* U) for s in axes(m.R, 1), a in axes(m.R, 2)]
        U′ = vec(maximum(Q, dims = 2))
        maximum(abs.(U′ - U)) < δ && return U′, argmax.(eachrow(Q))
        U = U′
    end
end
U, policy = solve(mdp)
@assert mdp.states[argmax(U)] == (2, 9)    # the +10 tile is worth the most
```
:::

::: {#27046408 .cell execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```

Most valuable tile: (2, 9) with U* = 10.00
```
:::

## Hex World {#hex-world}

**The story.** A robot crosses a floor of hexagonal tiles. Three tiles are special: one pays +10, one pays +5, and one costs −10. Acting on a special tile collects its value and ends the episode. The floor is slippery, so a move sometimes veers off course, and walking into the edge of the map wastes a turn and costs 1.

It is a good first benchmark because it is small enough to solve exactly (25 states), yet it has real trade-offs. The +5 is closer than the +10 for part of the map, and the −10 sits beside a useful path.

| | |
|---|---|
| States | 24 tiles, plus one terminal state reached after collecting a reward |
| Actions | Move in one of 6 directions: E, NE, NW, W, SW, SE |
| Rewards | +10, +5 and −10 on three tiles; −1 for bumping into the edge |
| Discount | $\gamma = 0.9$ |

: Hex World at a glance (ADM §F.1). {#tbl-hex}

::: {.key-equation data-name="Hex World transition model"}
$$
T(s' \mid s, a) = 0.7\,\big[s' = \mathrm{step}(s, a)\big] + 0.15\,\big[s' = \mathrm{step}(s, a^{-})\big] + 0.15\,\big[s' = \mathrm{step}(s, a^{+})\big]
$$ {#eq-hex-transition}
:::

**In words.** The robot goes the way it chose 70% of the time. Otherwise it veers 60° to the left or to the right, 15% each.

**Term by term.**

- $\mathrm{step}(s, a)$ is the tile one step from $s$ in direction $a$. If that step would leave the map, $\mathrm{step}(s, a) = s$: the robot stays put.
- $a^{-}$ and $a^{+}$ are the two directions next to $a$. For $a = \text{E}$ they are NE and SE.
- $[\cdot]$ is 1 if the condition inside is true and 0 otherwise, so the three terms add up the ways of landing on $s'$.
- On a reward tile, every action instead moves to the terminal state with probability 1.

The reward is $R(s, a) = r(s)$ on a reward tile. Elsewhere it is $-1$ times the probability of bumping into the edge. For example, heading east from the top-left tile veers off the map with probability 0.15, so $R = -0.15$.

@fig-hex-world shows the map and its optimal policy.

::: {#cell-fig-hex-world .cell execution_count=4}

![Hex World. Left: the map, with the three reward tiles colored. Right: the optimal values (color) and policy (arrows) from value iteration with γ = 0.9.](f-problems_files/figure-html/fig-hex-world-output-1.png){#fig-hex-world width=716 height=198 fig-alt='Two hex maps side by side, each with three rows of hexagonal tiles: ten on top, six in the middle, eight on the bottom. On the right map, every tile is shaded by its value, from pale near the −10 to darker blue near the +10, and arrows show the best move. Tiles in the left third point toward the +5, tiles in the right two-thirds point toward the +10, and no tile next to the −10 aims at it.'}

### Straight-line Hex World

A smaller variant has seven tiles in a row, with +10 on the rightmost tile. Its only purpose is to make one thing visible: how value iteration spreads reward backward, one tile per sweep (@fig-hex-line).

::: {#cell-fig-hex-line .cell execution_count=5}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Value iteration on straight-line Hex World (γ = 0.9). Each row is one sweep. The +10 reaches one more tile to the left per sweep, fading as it goes. Tiles it hasn't reached yet are slightly negative: in a single row every move risks veering off the edge, which costs 1. The values settle after 26 sweeps.](f-problems_files/figure-html/fig-hex-line-output-1.png){#fig-hex-line width=322 height=359 fig-alt='Seven stacked rows of seven hexagons each, labeled sweep 1 to sweep 7. By sweep 7 every tile except the leftmost is blue.'}

## Problems made for this site

The chapters also use small original problems, built to make one idea easy to see. The ones reused across pages get a full entry here, in both languages; the rest are listed in @tbl-originals.

### Morning commute {#morning-commute}

**The story.** Five yes/no facts about a morning: was there a storm, roadwork, a traffic jam; were you late; did the radio warn of a storm. Storms and roadwork cause jams, jams make you late, and storms trigger radio alerts. It is small enough to check every answer by hand, yet it contains all three d-separation patterns: a chain, a fork and a collider.

```{dot}

//| fig-width: 3.62
//| fig-height: 2.79
//| fig-cap: "The morning-commute Bayesian network."
//| fig-alt: "A directed graph with five boxes. Storm and Roadwork both point to Traffic jam, which points to Late. Storm also points to Radio alert."
digraph commute {
  bgcolor="#fcfcfb"; pad=0.2; nodesep=0.5; ranksep=0.45;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="white", color="#52514e", penwidth=1.2,
        fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=13, fontcolor="#0b0b0b"];
  edge [color="#52514e", penwidth=1.2, arrowsize=0.7];
  S [label="Storm (S)"]; R [label="Roadwork (R)"]; J [label="Traffic jam (J)"];
  L [label="Late (L)"]; A [label="Radio alert (A)"];
  S -> J; R -> J; J -> L; S -> A;
}
```

| Variable | Parents | P(yes \| parents) |
|---|---|---|
| Storm $S$ | — | 0.1 |
| Roadwork $R$ | — | 0.2 |
| Traffic jam $J$ | $S, R$ | 0.1 (neither), 0.6 (roadwork only), 0.7 (storm only), 0.9 (both) |
| Late $L$ | $J$ | 0.05 (no jam), 0.5 (jam) |
| Radio alert $A$ | $S$ | 0.02 (no storm), 0.95 (storm) |

## Python

::: {#2d93ed31 .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from adm.problems.commute import COMMUTE     # a BayesNet: card, parents, cpt
p_jam_given_storm_only = COMMUTE.cpt["J"][1, 0, 1]   # axes: S, R, then J; value 1 = yes
```
:::


## Julia
```{.julia .snippet}
using ADM
commute = commute_network()                   # a BayesNet: card, parents, cpt
@assert commute.cpt[:J][2, 1, 2] == 0.7       # axes: S, R, then J; value 2 = yes (1-based)
```
:::

**Where it's used.** [Ch 2](../part1/ch02-representation.qmd): the chain rule, parameter counts, explaining away, d-separation. [Ch 3](../part1/ch03-inference.qmd): every inference method answers $P(\text{storm} \mid \text{late}, \text{alert}) = 0.935$. [Ch 4](../part1/ch04-parameter-learning.qmd): its tables are learned back from simulated mornings, including with the storm value missing (EM).

### Coffee machine {#coffee-machine}

**The story.** An espresso machine is fine, has scale buildup, or has a worn pump. You can't see which, but you can notice three symptoms: slow flow, a loud noise, and weak-tasting coffee. Each symptom depends only on the machine's condition, which makes this a **naive Bayes** model. It shows how a rare cause can become the most likely one once the evidence fits it well.

::: {#tbl-gallery-coffee .cell tbl-cap='The coffee-machine model: prior over the condition and P(symptom present | condition).' execution_count=7}

| scale buildup | 0.15 | 0.70 | 0.20 | 0.60 |

### Commute times {#commute-times}

**The story.** Morning and evening commute times, in minutes, are jointly Gaussian: morning $\mathcal{N}(35, 8^2)$ and evening $\mathcal{N}(40, 10^2)$, with correlation $\rho = 0.6$, because a bad traffic day tends to be bad all day. It is the smallest example of conditioning a Gaussian: one observation shifts the other's mean and shrinks its spread.

| | Morning | Evening |
|---|---|---|
| Mean (min) | 35 | 40 |
| Standard deviation (min) | 8 | 10 |
| Covariance matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ | $\begin{pmatrix} 64 & 48 \\ 48 & 100 \end{pmatrix}$ | ($48 = 0.6 \times 8 \times 10$) |

: Commute times as a bivariate Gaussian. {#tbl-commute-times}

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
